newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO expansion to redraw Europe's security map.
newsitem.headline: NATO expansion to redraw Europe's security map.

text.p: NATO throws open its doors to former communist enemies next week, bringing the security map of Europe in line with the reality of the post-Cold War world and reinforcing the new democracies' break with Moscow.

A summit of NATO leaders in Madrid will invite at least Poland, the Czech Republic, and Hungary --- all former members of the now-defunct Warsaw Pact --- to join the West's defence shield, and offer close ties to a host of other applicants.
But the run-up to the summit, called to inaugurate a new NATO by endorsing wide-ranging internal and external changes, has been marred by disputes which threaten to take the shine off the event.

France and several other southern European members have fought strongly for the inclusion of Romania and Slovenia in a "first wave" of new members and been angered by the United States' preference, stated publicly, for the leading three.

The row, which goes to the heart of the arguments in favour of alliance expansion, may not be settled until just before the July 8-9 summit, leaving an impression of European Union-style horse-trading the alliance desperately wanted to avoid.
"I agree with the process of enlargement, but fundamentally disagree with the way in which it has been conducted," said Jonathan Eyal of London's Royal United Services Institute.

Eyal says that when the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) said it would expand eastwards it said countries would be admitted if they fulfilled certain criteria, such as creating market economies and settling disputes with neighbouring states.
"Of course enlargement was and is a political process and now it has come down to a rather unseemly oriental bazaar," he added.

Most independent analysts accept Romania and Slovenia have broadly fulfilled the membership conditions, which also include democratic control of the armed forces and respect of human rights, but will not make it for strategic and economic reasons.

Supporters argue enlargement will help erase for good the division of Europe, spread Europe's zone of stability further east and anchor former communist states firmly to a Western institution to which all democracies have a right to belong.

A growing and vocal band of critics, particularly in the U.S., say the expansion will weaken the most powerful military alliance ever created by making it unwieldly and spreading its mutual defence commitments too widely.

"Not to have enlarged would have effectively meant freezing the old lines of division, enlargement will fundamentally alter the security map of Europe by erasing the old split," said one senior alliance diplomatic source.
"That is in itself a strong argument in favour, but of course it does not directly provide additional security for the states that do not get in," he added.

NATO countries, committed to further rounds of enlargement, are currently wrangling over how to word the "open door" section of the communique to be issued in Madrid with countries in favour of wider enlargement wanting specific names and dates.
"There is a suggestion of the 'two-crested wave' -- three invited now, with two to come later," said Eyal.
NATO diplomats say there is a consensus over three countries joining and on leaving the door open for future enlargements, but little agreement from then on.

NATO's northern bloc, led by the Scandinavians, insist that the Baltic States of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia must be given equal treatment even though Russia would baulk at the prospect of former Soviet Republics joining the Western alliance.
"The Balts cannot be treated differently just because they were once forced to be part of the Soivet Union," Denmark's Defence Minister Hans Haekkerrup recently told Reuters.

NATO's enlargement is also intended to underline the alliance's role as the continent's paramount security organisation and the vehicle which gives concrete expression to the U.S. involvement in European security.
"Enlargement is not about securing NATO's future, but ensuring its relevance in a new Europe," said Simon Lunn,
